metric_rationale: In this specific experimental design, every single trial is constructed such that Take The Best (TTB) and Tallying predict strictly opposite choices. TTB favors the option that wins on the highest-validity discriminating cue, while Tallying favors the option that wins on a larger number of lower-validity cues. By calculating the proportion of trials where the participant's choice aligns with the TTB prediction, we can perfectly discriminate the two models: data generated by TTB will yield a metric value close to 1 (subject to noise), whereas data generated by Tallying will yield a metric value close to 0.

The experimental design consists of 8 trial types where the option with the highest validity cue (favored by Take The Best) is always opposed by the option with a higher number of winning cues (favored by Tallying). By measuring the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the Tallying-favored option, we obtain a metric that will be strictly greater than 0.5 under Tallying and strictly less than 0.5 under Take The Best. The large number of trials (96 per subject) ensures stable within-subject estimates, leading to low between-subject variance and a highly significant separation between the two theories.

By design, every trial in the experiment pits the single highest-validity discriminating cue (which always favors Option A) against multiple lower-validity cues (which favor Option B). Take The Best (TTB) strictly follows the highest-validity discriminating cue, so it predicts that subjects will almost always choose Option A (response = 0). Weighted Additive (WADD) integrates all cues, so for a wide range of its gamma parameter, the combined weight of the lower-validity cues will exceed the single high-validity cue, leading to choices for Option B (response = 1). The overall mean of the response column directly measures the proportion of compensatory (Option B) choices, which will be near 0 for TTB and significantly higher for WADD.

By design, every trial pits a single high-validity cue (favoring Option A) against multiple lower-validity cues (favoring Option B). Since TTB strictly follows the first discriminating cue, it will deterministically favor Option A on every trial, choosing B only through random lapses. In contrast, WADD's compensatory nature allows the sum of multiple lower-validity cues to outweigh the single high-validity cue for lower values of the gamma parameter. Measuring the overall proportion of Option B choices across all trials provides a highly stable, low-variance estimate of compensatory behavior, maximizing the quantitative dissociation between the two models.

The TTB/Tallying Mixture model relies on two invariant signals: the rank of the highest discriminating cue (for TTB) and the unweighted count of winning cues (for Tallying). In both Trial 6 and Trial 8, Option A and Option B each have exactly one cue, meaning Tallying is tied. Furthermore, in both trials, Option A's cue is higher in validity than Option B's, so TTB strictly prefers A. Because the Mixture model's TTB implementation is purely rank-based and ignores absolute validity magnitudes, it predicts exactly the same probability of choosing A in Trial 6 and Trial 8. Thus, the expected value of P(A|t6) - P(A|t8) is exactly 0 under the Mixture model.

In contrast, WADD integrates absolute validities using a power function (gamma). At moderate to high gamma values (which dominate the adversary's prior), the weights of lower-validity cues vanish exponentially toward zero. In Trial 6, the cues are the highest available (0.95 vs 0.85), so their difference remains large and WADD strongly prefers A (P(A) ~ 1.0). In Trial 8, the cues are much lower (0.75 vs 0.65). At high gamma, these values become infinitesimally small, making their absolute difference effectively zero. Consequently, WADD becomes indifferent and predicts a probability near 0.5 for Trial 8. This leads WADD to consistently predict a massive positive difference (often > 0.3) for P(A|t6) - P(A|t8), perfectly discriminating the two theories.

Theory 2 predicts a constant choice probability across all 8 trial types, as TTB and Tallying signals are structurally identical across pairs (A always wins TTB 1-0, B always wins Tallying 2-1). Thus, any variance in choice rates across the 8 trial types is purely due to binomial noise. Theory 1 (WADD) integrates the exact validities, predicting systematically different choice probabilities across the 8 pairs as the compensating cues shift from strong to weak. By calculating the standard deviation of the mean choice rates across the 8 trial types, we capture this difference: Theory 2 will have a low standard deviation (only noise), while Theory 1 will have a significantly higher standard deviation (true probability variance + noise).
